Building an explicit **graph over the corpus** tends to pay off when you have **(a) complex query structure** and/or **(b) scale-induced retrieval noise** such that “better organization” beats “more similarity search”—*and* when you can amortize the **indexing cost**.

From the corpus evidence:

- **As the corpus gets large, graph structure can stabilize retrieval/QA quality by reducing noise.** In GraphRAG-Bench results summarized in *When to use Graphs in RAG…*, a graph method (HippoRAG2) stays roughly flat on a complex-reasoning metric as the context/corpus grows from ~56k to 1.1M tokens, while vanilla RAG drops substantially (58.6% → 43.2%). The interpretation given is that the graph helps “filter retrieval noise” as scale increases. (paper.graph-rag-survey-2025#c7)

- **Graphs help more on “complex reasoning / sensemaking / summarization” than on simple fact lookup.** The same survey+benchmark page states the overall verdict: graphs “pay off on complex-reasoning/summarization tasks and at scale,” but “not for simple fact retrieval,” and warns that token costs can be **100–377×** vanilla RAG. (paper.graph-rag-survey-2025)

- **The economics are usually “indexing-heavy / query-light,” so you need enough queries per corpus.** The GSW paper’s practical notes generalize this: graph/memory-style indexes are a bigger upfront investment and only amortize with high query volume; it also suggests that for small corpora (≈ below ~10k tokens) you should skip the heavier memory/graph frameworks. (paper.gsw-2025#practical_notes)

- **Task/query shape is decisive (validate per task, not per method family).** The same practical notes report that for certain aggregation-style queries (“all events/locations/dates of entity X”), “every graph RAG loses to plain embedding RAG,” and rankings can flip relative to sensemaking benchmarks—so graphs aren’t a universal win even when they’re sophisticated. (paper.gsw-2025#practical_notes)

Synthesis: a corpus graph is most worth it when you’re doing **multi-hop/sensemaking-style questions over large corpora** where similarity search starts returning too much irrelevant stuff, and when you expect **enough repeated querying** to pay back the higher indexing (and often higher token) costs; it’s less likely to be worth it for **straight factoid retrieval**, **small corpora**, or **query types that don’t benefit from relational structure**. (paper.graph-rag-survey-2025, paper.graph-rag-survey-2025#c7, paper.gsw-2025#practical_notes, cmp.graph-rag-architectures)
